summary: Introduces a PCEP extension that associates a group of LSPs for the purpose of computing diverse (disjoint) paths. A client can tell a PCE that an LSP belongs to a given disjoint association group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8800 lets a client tell a path computer that several paths have to stay out of each other's way. The paths are put in a group, and a small set of flags says what they must not share: links, nodes, or groups of links that fail together. The path computer then plans them so that no single failure takes more than one of them down, and reports back what it achieved.

questions: how to compute disjoint lsps with pcep

what is the p flag in pcep disjointness
subtitle: How PCEP tells a path computation element that a group of LSPs must take different routes through the network.

tldr.problem: Operators often must give a customer two end-to-end paths that do not share links, nodes or fate, but PCEP had no standard way to say that a set of LSPs belong together and must be disjoint.
tldr.mechanism: A new Disjoint Association type for the ASSOCIATION object groups the LSPs, a DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV states what kind of disjointness is required, and a DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV reports what was achieved.
tldr.outcome: A PCE that sees LSPs in the same Disjoint Association Group can compute them to be disjoint, strictly or with relaxation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8800 is a Proposed Standard, and it is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The PCEP extensions for the stateful PCE model of RFC 8231 enable active control of MPLS-TE and GMPLS tunnels, and RFC 8281 describes the setup and teardown of PCE-initiated LSPs under that model, without the need for local configuration on the client. RFC 8697 introduces a generic mechanism to create a grouping of LSPs in the context of a PCE, which can then be used to define associations between a set of LSPs and a set of attributes such as configuration parameters or behaviours. It applies equally to the active and passive modes of a stateful PCE and to a stateless PCE.

This document specifies a PCEP extension to signal that a set of LSPs in a particular group should use diverse, or disjoint, paths, including the requested type of diversity. A client uses the extension to signal to a PCE that a particular LSP belongs to a particular Disjoint Association Group. When a PCE receives LSP states belonging to the same Disjoint Association Group from some clients, the PCE should ensure that the LSPs within the group are disjoint from each other.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP already lets a client ask a path computer to plan a set of paths that are related to each other. This RFC adds the case where the relation is that the paths must not share resources, so that a single failure cannot take them all down.

sections.title: Why Disjoint Paths
sections.content:
Path diversity is a very common use case in IP and MPLS networks, especially for layer 2 transport over MPLS. A customer may ask the operator for two end-to-end disjoint paths across the operator's IP and MPLS core, and may use them as a primary and backup pair or as an active and active pair.

The RFC names four levels of disjointness that may be offered.

  • Link disjointness: the paths of the associated LSPs should transit different links, but they may use common nodes, or different links that may have some shared fate.
  • Node disjointness: the paths should transit different nodes, but they may use different links that may have some shared fate.
  • SRLG disjointness: the paths should transit different links that do not share fate, but they may use common transit nodes. A Shared Risk Link Group, or SRLG, is the set of links that fail together.
  • Node and SRLG disjointness: the paths should transit different links that do not have any common shared fate, and should transit different nodes.

The associated LSPs may originate from the same or from different head ends, and may terminate at the same or at different tail ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Two paths can be kept apart in different ways. They can use different links, or different routers, or they can avoid the groups of links that fail together. A customer who needs two working paths across a provider's core asks for one of these levels, and the provider plans the pair to match it.

sections.title: The Disjoint Association Group
sections.content:
In RFC 8697, LSPs are associated with the other LSPs they interact with by adding them to a common association group, and the group is uniquely identified by the combination of the Association Type, the Association ID, the Association Source and, if present, the Global Association Source or the Extended Association ID.

This document defines a new association type, the Disjoint Association, of value 2, also called the Disjoint Association Type or DAT. The capability exchange for this type must be done before the disjoint association is used: a speaker must include the DAT in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV of the OPEN object and must receive the same from its peer before using a Disjoint Association Group in PCEP messages.

The association type is both dynamic and operator-configured in nature. The group can be created by the operator on the PCEP peers, with the LSPs belonging to it conveyed in PCEP messages, or it can be created dynamically by a speaker, which conveys both the group and its members. The operator-configured Association Range must be set for this association type, to mark a range of Association Identifiers used for operator-configured associations and avoid a clash within the scope of the Association Source.

A Disjoint Association Group can hold two or more LSPs, but a PCE may be limited in how many LSPs it can take into account when computing disjointness. If it receives more, it should apply the computation to only a subset, chosen by local policy, and local policies may define what happens to the others: the PCE may provide no path, a shortest path, or a constrained path based on relaxing disjointness. The status of the computed paths is reported back with the DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV.

All LSPs in one Disjoint Association Group must use the same combination of the T, S, N and L flags. If a peer receives a message for LSPs of the same group with an inconsistent combination, it must not add them to the group and must reply with a PCEP error of Error-Type 26, Association Error, and Error-value 6, association information mismatch. An LSP may belong to more than one Disjoint Association Group, and the PCE should consider all of them during path computation. If the PCE does not support that computation, it must not add the LSP to the group and must return Error-Type 26 with Error-value 7, cannot join the association group.
sections.plainLanguage: The group is identified by four values, one of which is the kind of grouping: this one means the paths must be disjoint. Before using it, the two ends exchange the list of grouping kinds they support. Every path in the same group must ask for the same kind of disjointness, and a path that asks for something different is refused with an error.

sections.title: The Disjointness TLVs
sections.content:
The Disjoint Association Group must carry the DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV, which communicates the disjointness configuration parameters and applies to every PCEP message that includes the group. It may also carry the DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV, which reports the status of the computed disjointness and applies only to messages from a PCE to a client, that is PCUpd, PCInitiate or PCRep; the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV of RFC 7470 for vendor-specific information; and the OF-List TLV, which carries the disjointness objective function.

The DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV has type 46 and a fixed length of 4 bytes, and its value is a 32-bit flags field. The L bit, Link Diverse, means the computed paths must not have any link in common. The N bit, Node Diverse, means they must not have any node in common. The S bit, SRLG Diverse, means they must not share any SRLG. The P bit, Shortest Path, means the computed path should satisfy all the other constraints and objective functions first, without considering the diversity constraint: the LSPs with the P flag set are computed first as if the disjointness constraint had not been configured, and then the other LSPs in the group are computed with the disjointness constraint applied. The T bit, Strict Disjointness, means that if disjoint paths cannot be found, the PCE must return no path for the LSPs that could not be made disjoint; when it is clear, the PCE may relax disjointness by applying a requested objective function or, if none is requested, by local policy, for example by using a lower disjoint type such as link instead of node, or by relaxing the constraint fully. The unassigned bits are reserved, must be set to 0 on transmission and must be ignored on receipt.

If a speaker receives a Disjoint Association Group without the DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV, it should reply with a PCEP error of Error-Type 6, mandatory object missing, and Error-value 15.

The DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV uses the same format with a different type, 47. The L, N and S flags are set when the corresponding criterion was requested and the computed paths meet it, and the P flag indicates that the computed path is the shortest path, computed first without the disjointness constraint but with the other constraints applied. The T flag has no meaning in the status TLV, must not be set when sending, and must be ignored on receipt. Any document that defines a new flag for the configuration TLV automatically defines the same flag in the status TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Two small blocks of flags travel with the group. One says what is required: no shared links, no shared nodes, no shared failure groups, and whether the result must be strict or may be relaxed. The other says what was achieved. A fourth flag marks one path in the group as the one that should get the best route, with the others then kept away from it.

sections.title: Disjointness Objective Functions
sections.content:
An objective function may be applied to the disjointness computation to drive the behaviour of the path computer, using the OF-List TLV of RFC 5541 as an optional TLV in the ASSOCIATION object. Although that TLV allows several objective function codes, a sender should include a single code in it when it is used in an association group, and the receiver must consider the first code only and ignore any others.

Three new objective functions are defined to minimize the resources shared between a set of paths. MSL, Minimize the number of Shared (common) Links, has code 15 and finds a set of paths that passes through the least number of links common to more than one path. MSS, Minimize the number of Shared (common) SRLGs, has code 16 and does the same for shared risk link groups. MSN, Minimize the number of Shared (common) Nodes, has code 17 and does the same for shared nodes.

If the OF-List TLV is present in the ASSOCIATION object, the first objective function code it holds must be one of these three. If it is not, the speaker must respond with a PCEP error of Error-Type 10, reception of an invalid object, and Error-value 32, incompatible OF code.
sections.plainLanguage: When a strict disjoint set cannot be found, the path computer can instead find a set that shares as little as possible. Three rules are offered: share as few links as possible, as few failure groups as possible, or as few routers as possible. The client names one of them, and it has to be one of these three.

sections.title: How This Works with the SVEC Object and the Shortest Path Flag
sections.content:
RFC 5440 defines the SVEC object for synchronizing a set of path computation requests, identifying them by the Request-ID-number in the Request Parameters object. A request may use both the SVEC object and the ASSOCIATION object to identify the related requests and the disjoint group, and the PCE must try to find a path that meets both sets of constraints. The diversity requirement in the group may differ from the one in the SVEC object, and the PCE must consider both, including the flags inside them. If no path meets both, the PCE must send a Path Computation Reply with a NO-PATH object. The LSPs in the group may be the same as, or partly overlapping with, the LSPs grouped by the SVEC object.

The P flag says that the path of that LSP should satisfy all the other constraints and objective functions first, without considering the diversity constraint, so it is placed first as if disjointness had not been asked for, and the other LSPs in the group are then placed with the disjointness constraint applied. Setting the P flag makes the relationship one-sided: an LSP with P=0 depends on an LSP with P=1, but not the other way round. Several LSPs in the same group may have the P flag set, and those may not be disjoint from each other, though they will be disjoint from the LSPs in the group that do not have it set.

The RFC works this through an example. A customer with two dual-homed sites wants two link-disjoint paths, and wants the path between the first pair of sites to use the best route available. Without the hint, the PCE may compute the two paths together in a way that satisfies disjointness but leaves the first path on a worse route. With the P flag set on the first path, the PCE uses the path PE1 to R1 to R3 to R4 to R2 to PE2 for it, and the second path is placed on PE3 to R5 to R6 to PE4, where it is allowed to be costlier. The RFC also notes that the P flag, like any other extra constraint, lowers the chance of finding a disjoint set, and that where several equal-cost paths exist, an implementation should aim to pick one that still allows disjointness.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mechanisms work together here. The SVEC object groups requests that are computed together, and the association group groups paths that must be kept apart; the path computer has to satisfy both. The shortest path flag marks one path in the group as the one that should get the best available route, and the other paths are then fitted around it, which is what a customer with a primary and a backup usually wants.

sections.title: When Disjoint Paths Cannot Be Found
sections.content:
There are cases where the PCE cannot provide a set of disjoint paths for one or more LSPs in the association.

When the T flag is set, meaning strict disjointness, and disjointness cannot be ensured for one or more LSPs, the PCE must reply to a request with a reply message containing a NO-PATH object. In the case of a state report, it must return a PCEP error of Error-Type 26, Association Error, and Error-value 7, cannot join the association group.

In the case of a network event that makes strict disjointness impossible, the PCE must send an update message containing an empty Explicit Route Object to the corresponding clients, and may add the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV of RFC 5440 in the LSP object. This document adds two bits in the flags field of that TLV: bit 11 indicates that the PCE could not find a disjoint path for the LSP, and bit 10 indicates that it does not support the requested disjointness computation.

When the T flag is clear, the PCE may relax disjointness by applying a requested objective function, or, if no objective function was specified, by reducing the required level of disjointness as it sees fit, for instance by falling back from node disjointness to link disjointness. The level actually achieved is reported through the DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV: the configuration TLV states the level that was asked for, and the status TLV states the level that was computed. A mechanism that would let the PCE relax a constraint completely, for every kind of request rather than for this one, is considered out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Strict mode means that if the paths cannot be kept apart, the answer is that there is no path. The loose mode lets the path computer give a best effort, for example by keeping the paths on different routers even if they share a link, and it then reports in the status flags how much separation it actually achieved.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new association type adds no security concerns of its own beyond those discussed in RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 7470 and RFC 8697. Adding a spurious LSP to a Disjoint Association Group could lead to recomputation and setup of all the LSPs in the group, which could be used to overwhelm the PCE and the network. A spurious LSP can carry flags inconsistent with those of the legitimate LSPs of the group and so make the allocation for the legitimate LSPs fail with an error, and certain combinations of flags, notably the T bit, can produce conflicts that cannot be resolved.

Much of the information in the ASSOCIATION object reflects information that can also be derived from the LSP database, but the association gives an easier grouping of related LSPs and messages. That holds for the Disjoint Association Type as well, so it could give an adversary the opportunity to eavesdrop on the relationship between the LSPs and understand the network topology. Securing the PCEP session with Transport Layer Security, following the recommendations and best current practices of BCP 195, is therefore recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The grouping itself does not add new risks, but it can be abused: a path added to a group without permission would force the path computer to plan the whole group again, and the grouping also reveals which paths belong together, which helps someone map the network. The RFC therefore recommends protecting the session with TLS.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Code point 46 for the configuration TLV; the status TLV uses 47.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 31 link diverse, bit 30 node diverse, bit 29 SRLG diverse, bit 28 shortest path, bit 27 strict disjointness.

viz.caption: The five flags of the configuration TLV

items.label: L, Link Diverse
items.desc: The paths in the group must not have any link in common.

items.label: N, Node Diverse
items.desc: The paths in the group must not have any node in common.

items.label: S, SRLG Diverse
items.desc: The paths in the group must not share any shared risk link group.

items.label: P, Shortest Path
items.desc: This path is computed first, without the diversity constraint applied.

items.label: T, Strict Disjointness
items.desc: If disjoint paths cannot be found, the PCE must return no path.

items.label: MSL
items.desc: Minimize the number of shared links across a set of paths.

items.label: MSS
items.desc: Minimize the number of shared SRLGs across a set of paths.

items.label: MSN
items.desc: Minimize the number of shared nodes across a set of paths.

viz.caption: The four levels of disjointness the RFC names

items.title: Link disjointness
items.text: The paths use different links, but may use common nodes or links that share fate.

items.title: Node disjointness
items.text: The paths use different nodes, but may use links that share fate.

items.title: SRLG disjointness
items.text: The paths use links that do not share fate, but may use common transit nodes.

items.title: Node and SRLG disjointness
items.text: The paths use different nodes and links that have no common shared fate.

viz.caption: Who starts the disjoint set and who enforces it

left.title: Initiated by the PCE
left.desc: The path computer starts the paths with an initiate message and enforces the disjointness itself.

right.title: Initiated by the PCC
right.desc: The client starts the paths and the path computer enforces the disjointness.

data.joiner: and enforced by the other end
